title: The Udasis
hookLine: an ascetic order tracing itself to Sri Chand, which cared for many gurdwaras in hard times

lines: A FAMILY LEAVES IN A HURRY.
cards: A family leaves home in a hurry, and a neighbor promises to look after the house. Months go by, then years. The neighbor waters the plants, sweeps the step, opens the windows on hot days so the place can breathe.
When the family finally comes back, the lamp in the front room is still lit. Nobody stood guard with a weapon. Somebody just kept showing up.
The Sikh panth tells a story with that shape about its own shrines, and the neighbors in it belong to an order you met in year three, through the Guru's son.

teach.h: AN ORDER TRACED TO BABA SRI CHAND.
teach.b: The Udasis are an order of renunciants. They trace themselves to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, who chose a celibate life of meditation, as year three told.
Udasi teachers kept Guru Nanak's hymns at the center of their devotion, and tradition remembers the later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect.

teach.h: THE HARD YEARS: KHALSA SIKHS HUNTED.
teach.b: Year three also walked through the years when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted, living in forests and on horseback, unable to stay safely near their own shrines.
Tradition says that in those years Udasi caretakers looked after many gurdwaras. They didn't wear the Khalsa's outward form, so they could stay where Khalsa Sikhs could not.
They kept the doors open, the lamps lit, and the Guru's word read. There's a second chapter.
Tradition also remembers that, much later, at some shrines the hereditary caretakers grew wealthy and careless, and a reform movement brought those shrines back under the panth's own care.
That story comes on another day; hold both chapters together, and let neither erase the other. Last, a line from Guru Nanak close to the word udasi, which carries the sense of being detached.

teach.h: THE LOTUS UNTOUCHED BY THE WATER.
teach.b: In the conversation with the Siddhas, the yogis of the mountains, he gives a picture of detachment, in paraphrase: like a lotus that floats untouched by the water, like a duck that swims the stream and stays dry.
The Udasis chose a renunciant's road to seek that freedom.
In the hard years, their freedom from house and household left them free to keep the Guru's house.

how: Sikhs remember the Udasis as caretakers of many gurdwaras in the years when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted, and hold a range of views about the order's place in the panth today.

games.q: you're an Udasi caretaker in the hard years. riders of the Khalsa can't come near the shrine you live beside. what do you do?
o: lock the doors and leave until it's safe.
keep the doors open, the lamp lit and the Guru's word read.
hand the keys to whoever rules the town.
games.why: tradition says Udasi caretakers stayed and kept many gurdwaras going: lamps lit, doors open, the Guru's word read.

practice: Bring to mind someone who quietly kept something going, a grandparent who held the family's prayers, a caretaker at a place of worship, and see what they kept and what might have been lost without them.
Breathe in their name and breathe out a little thanks, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Udasi. A renunciant order tracing itself to Baba Sri Chand. Tradition says Udasi caretakers kept many gurdwaras open when Khalsa Sikhs could not. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: one who is detached, a renunciant. Guru Nanak's great journeys are also called his udasis.

carryVoice: Your line: keepers in hard times. Sometimes faithfulness looks like a lamp that is simply never let go out. Day thirteen-oh-three, done.
